title: Tennessee Inmate Christa Pike Hospitalized After Botched Execution
text:
Christa Pike, the first woman set for execution in Tennessee since 1819, is in critical condition after a failed lethal injection; Governor Bill Lee orders a third-party review.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in critical condition at a local hospital after a botched execution on Wednesday night, during which she survived two lethal injection s. Pike, who was scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1819, was given an all-female lethal injection team at her request, her attorneys revealed on Thursday. The execution was initially set for 10:00 a.m. on Wednesday but was delayed; a federal appeals court granted a stay a little more than an hour before it was to take place, after witnesses had already gathered at the Nashville prison.
Failed Execution and Hospitalization
According to her attorneys, the drugs may have been injected into the muscle of Pike's arm instead of a vein. Attorney Stephen Ferrell noted that this could have caused the execution to fail. After the failed attempt, Pike was transported to a local hospital where she remains in critical condition. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not released further details on her current health status.
In the hours following the failed execution, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee released a statement saying he has ordered a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred. The review will examine the protocols and procedures used during the execution. The governor's office has not provided a timeline for the review's completion.
Victim's Family Reacts to Failed Execution
The family of Colleen Slemmer, the victim in the case, expressed frustration and anger over the situation. Slemmer's mother, Martinez, criticized Pike for what she described as playing the system. She stated that Pike should not receive any special treatment and that Pike did not consider how her daughter felt. Martinez recounted that during the execution, officials asked the victims to leave without explanation, and they only learned later that the execution had failed. She said they were told that it did not work and that Pike was on her way to the hospital.
Pike was convicted of torturing and killing her Job Corps classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage 31 years ago. The case has been a long-standing capital punishment matter in Tennessee. Pike's attorneys have argued that she was a victim of sexual abuse, and that her biggest fear was being pinned down, prodded, poked, and cut during the execution process.
Legal and Legislative Context
The failed execution has raised questions about Tennessee's lethal injection protocols and the training of execution staff. Attorney Randy Spivey, when asked whether the execution staff was made up solely of women, said that what he saw was consistent with that. The all-female team was requested by Pike, according to her legal representation.
The federal appeals court stay that was granted shortly before the execution was part of ongoing legal challenges. The stay was issued after witnesses had already gathered at the Nashville prison, leading to confusion among those present. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not commented on the specifics of the stay or the subsequent execution attempt.
Governor Lee's order for a third-party review indicates the seriousness with which the state is treating the incident. The review is expected to determine whether the execution team followed proper procedures and whether any changes are needed to prevent similar occurrences in the future. The outcome could impact how Tennessee conducts executions going forward.
Background on Christa Pike Case
Christa Pike was convicted in 1996 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. The two were classmates at a Job Corps center in Knoxville, Tennessee. According to court records, Pike and another individual tortured and killed Slemmer in a jealous rage over a boyfriend. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 and has been on death row since then. Her case has been through numerous appeals over the past three decades.
If the execution had been carried out, Pike would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee since 1819. The state has executed only a handful of women in its history. The failed execution has drawn national attention and renewed debate over capital punishment and lethal injection methods. The hospital where Pike is being treated has not released her condition, citing privacy laws. Her attorneys have not provided an update on her health since Thursday.
